lines: There is a message on your phone that you have not opened. You know the one. Maybe it says, we need to talk. Maybe it is from the doctor, or the bank, or your boss.
You saw the first line. Your stomach turned to ice. And you put the phone face down.
That was three days ago. And every hour since, it has been sitting there, getting heavier.
This film is about fear. Not the fear of lions. The fear of opening things. And about some very old words that might help.
In nineteen sixty five, Frank Herbert published a novel called Dune. Early in the story, a fifteen year old boy is told to put his hand into a box that fills it with pain, and not pull away.
He gets through it by repeating these words.
I must not fear.
Fear is the mind-killer.
Fear is the little-death that brings total obliteration.
I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me, and through me.
And when it has gone past, I will turn the inner eye, to see its path.
Where the fear has gone, there will be nothing.
Only I will remain.
The mind-killer. That is not only poetry. It is close to a description.
When your brain detects a threat, it shifts power away from the part that thinks, plans, and sees clearly, toward older circuits built for one thing. Survive the next ten seconds.
That was perfect for a lion. But your alarm cannot tell a lion from an email. So it fires at a subject line, and you lose exactly the part of you that could have handled it.
And much of what reaches your screen is built to keep it firing. In a study of over a hundred thousand headline variations, every extra negative word made a headline more likely to be clicked.
A frightened mind is a small mind. It cannot love, or create, or choose. It can only flinch.
Herbert did not invent this. He was writing down something humanity has been telling itself for thousands of years.
In the Hebrew Bible: Fear not, for I am with you.
In the Quran, God says to Moses and his brother: Fear not. I am with you both. I hear, and I see.
In the Bhagavad Gita, when the qualities of a godly life are listed, the very first one is fearlessness.
In Buddhist and Hindu art across Asia, there is a gesture. A raised, open hand. It is called abhaya. It means: do not be afraid.
The opening words of Sikh scripture describe the divine in a handful of words. One of them is: without fear.
A Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Nachman, put it like this. The whole world is a very narrow bridge. And the main thing is not to be afraid.
And in the New Testament, one line goes further than all of them. Perfect love casts out fear.
Look closely at these, and you will notice something. They almost never say, be brave.
They say: do not fear, for I am with you.
The answer to fear is not strength. It is company.
Science found the same thing, in a brain scanner. People waiting for an electric shock showed a weaker threat response when someone they loved was holding their hand.
Whatever you believe, the shape is the same. Fear is loudest when you are alone with it.
Now look at what the litany actually tells you to do. It does not say, feel no fear. It says: I will face it. I will let it pass over me, and through me.
Fear is a wave. It rises. It peaks. And if you stay, it falls.
But most of us never see the fall. We leave at the top. We close the app. We change the subject. We put the phone face down.
And each time we run, the brain learns one thing. That was dangerous, and running saved me. So next time, the wave is taller.
Staying teaches it something else. Therapists call this exposure, and it is one of the most reliable tools we have. You stay with the feared thing, and your brain learns: I can survive this.
Permit it to pass through you. That is the whole instruction.
And then comes the strangest promise in the litany. Where the fear has gone, there will be nothing.
Most of what we fear never arrives. In one study, people with chronic worry wrote down their worries, and tracked what happened. About nine in ten never came true.
And when the feared thing did happen, a later study found, people coped better than they had expected, more than eight times out of ten.
A real problem has edges. You can do something with it. A fear has none.
So open the message.
Sometimes it is nothing. Sometimes it is hard. Either way, the ice in your stomach was never the message. It was the not knowing.
Only I will remain. You, with your mind back.
So here is a small litany of your own, for this week.
One. Name it. Finish the sentence: I am afraid that. Out loud, or on paper.
Two. Breathe out slowly, and say: this is fear. It will pass through me.
Three. Do not be alone with it. Tell one person. Or pray, if you pray. Or hold a hand.
Four. Open one thing. The message. The letter. The bank app. Two minutes. And stay.
Five. Afterwards, turn the inner eye. Look at where the fear went. And notice what is still standing.
Fear will come back. It is supposed to. It is trying to keep you alive.
But it was never meant to drive.
For thousands of years, people have been raising an open hand to each other, and saying the same two words.
Fear not.
I will face my fear. I will permit it to pass over me, and through me.
Only I will remain.
The words and studies behind this film are on screen.
